opus-5.5.text:
I have a lot of respect for what Anthropic has done in interpretability. They've treated it as a serious scientific program rather than a side project. Work like the superposition papers, sparse autoencoders for extracting features, and more recently circuit tracing in large models has shaped how the whole field thinks. They showed you can open up a model and find concepts that are surprisingly human-readable, and that's a big deal.

My own perspective differs a little, partly because of my background in physics. Anthropic's approach is mostly post hoc. You train a huge model as a black box, then build tools like a microscope to look inside and reverse-engineer what it learned. That's valuable, and with frontier models it may be the only option. But it's a bit like doing biology: the system is already there, it's messy, and you try to make sense of it after the fact.

I've been more interested in the complementary direction: can we design models that are interpretable from the start? That was part of the motivation behind Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks. Physicists don't just observe nature. We look for representations in which the laws become simple. So I'd like the architecture or the training process to encourage modularity and sparsity, so the structure is easier to read. Interpretability by design, rather than only interpretability by dissection.

I don't see these as competing. I see them as two ends of the same bridge. Anthropic is digging from the side of the giant models people actually deploy, and some of us are digging from the side of small, clean, principled systems. Hopefully we meet in the middle.

One concern I'd raise, about the whole field and not just Anthropic, is how we know the explanations are right. Sparse autoencoders give you features, but there's always a question of whether you're discovering the model's true mechanism or imposing your own lens on it. In physics we have experiments to falsify theories. Interpretability still needs better standards for what counts as a correct explanation. I think that's the next big step, and Anthropic is well placed to push on it given their resources and their commitment to the problem.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Anthropic deserves a lot of credit for taking interpretability seriously as a core research direction rather than as an afterthought. Their mechanistic interpretability work, especially the line that went from understanding small transformer circuits to sparse autoencoders and dictionary learning on production-scale models, showed that you can actually find meaningful, human-understandable features inside these systems. That was not obvious a few years ago. Many people assumed the internals would be hopelessly entangled.

That said, I would describe their approach as very bottom-up. You take the network as given, you look at activations and weights, and you try to reverse-engineer what it is doing. It is a bit like neuroscience: you are studying an organism you did not design. My own interest, with things like Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks and the physics-inspired work, comes from the opposite direction. Can we design architectures that are interpretable by construction, where the structure itself tells you something, so you do not have to do so much archaeology afterward?

I do not think these are competing views. The reality is that the most capable models today are large transformers, and someone has to understand them as they are. Anthropic is doing that hard, unglamorous work, and they publish it openly, which matters. But there are real open questions. Features found with sparse autoencoders are correlational; whether they give you causal, reliable control over behavior at scale is still being tested. And there is a scaling worry: the models grow faster than our ability to interpret them, so interpretability needs its own scaling laws, in a sense.

So my assessment is positive but with a caveat. They have shown interpretability is a real science, not just visualization. The question for the field is whether understanding can keep up with capability, and I think answering that will require both their reverse-engineering approach and more forward-engineering ideas about building systems we can understand from the start.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a valuable direction. Instead of judging a model only by its answers, they’re trying to understand what happens inside it: what information it represents and how those representations contribute to its behavior.

The challenge is distinguishing an interpretation that sounds plausible from an explanation that actually predicts what the model will do. If you think you’ve identified a mechanism, can you intervene on it and produce the change you expected? Does that explanation still hold across different inputs?

So I’m positive about the approach, but I’d be cautious about equating an interpretable feature with a complete understanding. Finding useful pieces is progress; understanding how those pieces work together is a much bigger task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a valuable direction. If we want to understand why a model behaves a certain way, looking only at its answers isn’t enough. We also want to understand what computations inside the model produce those answers.

But I would distinguish finding an interesting internal pattern from actually explaining a mechanism. If you identify something that appears to represent a concept, can you intervene on it and predict how the model’s behavior will change? Does that explanation hold across different inputs? Those are stronger tests.

So I’m optimistic about the approach, but I think we should be careful about how much understanding we claim. The goal should be explanations that let us make reliable predictions, not just interpretations that sound plausible.
